parts.description: An aged dark-brown wooden yoke-like frame with a long carved curved beam, vertical supports, and rounded end holes. It has worn leather straps, rusted iron rings, rivets, and scuffed varnished surfaces.
parts.reasoning: The visible object is dominated by aged hardwood, with smaller contributions from leather straps and iron/steel rings, rivets, and side bands. No product data is provided, so dimensions and mass are estimated visually: approximately 1.5–1.7 m long, 0.35–0.45 m deep, and 0.65–0.80 m high including the hanging frame members. The main carved top beam appears to be a thick, irregular solid wooden member, while the lower vertical supports and loop-like members add additional wood volume but leave substantial open space. A plausible total wood volume is about 0.027–0.032 m^3; using aged hardwood density around 600–700 kg/m^3 gives roughly 17–22 kg of wood. Rusted iron rings, brackets, rivets, and leather straps likely add about 3–5 kg, so a total mass estimate of 22 kg is appropriate for a single rigid body representation. The root material is set to aged hardwood because it is the dominant structural and contact surface; the density is therefore the material density of the dominant wood rather than an effective density based on the large empty bounding box. Wood-on-general-surface friction is moderate to high, but the worn varnish and polished/scuffed high points reduce it slightly; static friction is estimated at 0.55 and dynamic friction at 0.45. Restitution is low-to-moderate at 0.35 because aged wood has limited bounce and the attached leather/metal hardware dissipates energy. The asset is highly concave, with open loops, holes, straps, and a central ring, so a single convex hull would greatly overfill the object and create unrealistic contacts. Convex decomposition is the best default PhysX choice for a dynamic rigid body: use separate convex pieces for the long carved beam, vertical wooden members, lower loop members, straps, and approximated ring sections. SDF mesh collision could be considered only if very high-fidelity concave contact is required and performance cost is acceptable; triangle mesh collision should be avoided for a freely moving dynamic body. A small rest offset of 0.001 m and contact offset of 0.01 m are recommended for meter-scale geometry to avoid jitter while keeping contacts visually close to the worn wood surface. CCD is enabled because the object has thin ring/strap features that can tunnel through surfaces during drops or fast manipulation; it can be disabled for purely slow, quasi-static scenes. The initial velocity is zero. For stable heavy-object contact, 120 Hz simulation is recommended, especially when the convex decomposition has many small parts. If the object is only a static display asset, hibernation/sleeping can be aggressive; for dynamic use, use moderate sleep thresholds and avoid very high initial angular velocities because the long, uneven mass distribution can produce large contact impulses.
